title: ShallowPPL: Investigating Early-Exit Logit Lens for Code Context Compression

raw.stage1:
### Reasoning:

#### Purpose:
The contribution's purpose is to investigate whether expensive full-depth perplexity scoring in LongCodeZip can be replaced by cheaper intermediate-layer scoring for code context compression. This objective focuses on optimizing computational efficiency while maintaining performance in code compression tasks. None of the prior papers explicitly address this specific purpose. While several papers discuss prompt compression (e.g., [1], [4], [5], [7], [8], [11], [20]), they focus on general prompt compression or natural language tasks rather than the specific investigation of replacing full-depth perplexity scoring with intermediate-layer scoring for code compression.

#### Mechanism:
The mechanism, ShallowPPL, truncates forward passes at layer L and projects intermediate representations to vocabulary space via the logit lens to approximate AMI-based code relevance scoring. Paper [2] introduces LogitLens4LLMs, which extends the logit lens technique to modern LLMs, enabling the projection of intermediate representations to vocabulary space. This is substantively equivalent to the mechanism described in the contribution, as both use the logit lens to project intermediate representations for analysis. Paper [14] also discusses the tuned lens, a refinement of the logit lens technique, which similarly decodes hidden states into distributions over the vocabulary. Both papers cover the underlying primitive of using the logit lens for intermediate-layer analysis.

#### Evaluation:
The evaluation uses pre-registered criteria (>=1.5x speedup, <=1.0 point quality drop) on Long Code Completion and RepoQA. Paper [12] evaluates code compression across multiple benchmarks (e.g., HumanEval, MBPP, MultiPL-E) and metrics, which aligns with the evaluation design of benchmarking compression techniques for code tasks. Paper [5] evaluates CodePromptZip on retrieval-augmented generation for coding tasks, which also involves benchmarking compression methods for code-related applications. Both papers use similar evaluation designs (benchmarking compression techniques for code tasks), making the evaluation facet covered.

#### Domain:
The domain of the contribution is repository-level code context compression. Paper [5] explicitly addresses code-specific prompt compression for retrieval-augmented generation in coding tasks, which falls within the same general application area of code context compression. Paper [12] also focuses on code compression, validating across multiple code benchmarks. Both papers operate in the same domain of code context compression, making this facet covered.
